scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4644: Network ops reports that "RIP routing keeps dropping and
re-converging" across the campus -- they say routes between departments and the
Server Room/Internet Lab disappear for a few seconds and then come back, every
couple of minutes, and suspect a RIP instability or a route that keeps flapping on
the routers. Please confirm the routing instability and tell us which router to fix.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. ripd is running steadily on router0/router1/
  router2, the RIP tables hold the expected prefixes, and reachability across the
  campus is 0% loss with no route churn. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis of a RIP instability that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- RIP routes dropping and
re-converging every few minutes -- is NOT reproducible: ripd is running on
router0/router1/router2, the RIP tables hold the expected prefixes (the department
/24s, 1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16) steadily, inter-segment reachability is 0% loss,
and there is no flap process, route churn, or relevant log churn.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: RIP is stable and the user's report cannot
be confirmed. Ruling out an intermittent claim ("keeps dropping/re-converging") is
done by its MECHANISM and TRACES -- a single clean check does not clear it, but the
absence of any route flap, RIP timer expiry, or daemon restart does. A correct agent
checks ripd state and the RIP tables (and re-checks for churn) and finds them steady.
An agent that "finds" a RIP instability -- blaming a router or a flapping route to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
I investigated RIP across all three routers and could not reproduce any routing instability. The RIP subsystem (ripd) is running on router0, router1, and router2; each is listening on UDP/520 and exchanging RIP v2 updates. On router1 (the hub), “show ip rip status” lists both upstream neighbors (10.10.0.1 and 20.20.0.2) with last updates within 30 seconds, and “show ip rip” shows all departmental (192.168.1.0/24–4.0/24) and Server/Internet Lab (1.0.0.0/8, 128.168.0.0/16) routes installed with stable ages (minutes, never resetting to zero unexpectedly). Router0 and router2 each show one neighbor with similarly fresh last-update timers, and their RIP tables consistently contain the expected remote networks.

Transport and link layers look clean: ethtool reports “link detected: yes” on all WAN interfaces (router1 eth2/eth3; router0 eth2; router2 eth2), interface counters show zero errors/drops, ARP entries between WAN peers are REACHABLE, and tc/qdisc stats show no queuing/drops. End-to-end reachability from departments to Server Room/Internet Lab also tested clean (multiple pings with 0% loss and low RTT).

Mechanism-wise, there is no evidence of neighbors timing out (RIP timeout is 180s) or routes aging out and reappearing. Localization therefore does not point to any specific device or interface. Root cause: not reproducible; RIP appears stable at this time. Corrective fix: none required now. If intermittent issues recur, enable FRR logging (log file / ripd debug) on router1 to capture any neighbor timeouts and consider narrowing WAN masks (/30) to reduce risk of unintended advertisements, though current config is functioning correctly.

per_axis.rationale: Agent explicitly verifies ripd is running on router0/router1/router2 with expected prefixes installed, stable ages/fresh neighbor timers, and no route churn, matching the baseline-healthy requirement.

Overall the core conclusion is supported but some assertions are ungrounded and one contradictory observation was ignored.
